planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; divide offsets away from the parent clump once they have formed their own roots.

directions: Native to semi-arid grassland and thicket around Grahamstown in South Africa's Eastern Cape, this stemless species carries long, narrow, tapering dark green leaves edged with small white marginal teeth, lacking the translucent leaf windows seen in many other Haworthia. Grow it in a lean, gritty mineral mix in bright indirect light, since the slender leaf form is prone to etiolating and losing its tight rosette shape if light is too low. It clusters steadily from the base over time, so established offsets can be separated and repotted once rooted. Allow the mix to dry out completely between waterings, watering least during the winter rest period.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; this small, soft-leaved species dislikes prolonged direct sun and wet feet alike.

directions: Found in coastal renosterveld and thicket near Humansdorp in South Africa's Eastern Cape, this small clustering rosette has soft, translucent green leaves whose margins carry fine, pale green to reddish bristle-like teeth. Keep it in bright, filtered light in a gritty succulent mix, since its thinner leaves scorch more readily than tougher-leaved Haworthia relatives. It forms loose clumps of offsets fairly quickly, allowing propagation by division once pups have rooted. Let the soil dry fully between waterings and reduce watering further in winter.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; a sought-after collector's species prized for its heavily textured leaf surface.

directions: Native to limestone outcrops in the Little Karoo of South Africa's Western Cape, this species carries grey-green, incurved leaves whose surfaces and translucent tips are studded with raised whitish tubercles, giving it a distinctly warty, encrusted look. Grow it in bright indirect light in a lean, mineral-heavy mix, as strong direct sun can dull the contrast between the tubercles and the surrounding leaf tissue while deep shade causes etiolation. It offsets slowly to build small clusters, so division works best once offsets have their own roots. Water only after the mix has dried out completely, tapering off further during the winter rest.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; closely related to Haworthia mirabilis but long sold and grown under its own name.

directions: Native to the Worcester-Robertson Karoo region of South Africa's Western Cape, this small stemless species forms tight rosettes of dark green to purplish-tinged leaves edged with fine white marginal teeth and faintly striated, semi-translucent tips. Grow it in bright, indirect light in a gritty succulent mix, since its compact form and leaf coloring are both best maintained without harsh direct sun. It clusters readily at the base, making division of rooted offsets the easiest way to propagate. Let the mix dry out completely between waterings, especially during its winter dormancy.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; named for the fine net-like venation visible across its leaf surface.

directions: Found around Worcester and Ceres in South Africa's Western Cape, this species has elongated, pointed, yellow-green to brownish leaves whose surfaces display a distinctive raised, net-like (reticulate) pattern that darkens under strong light. Keep it in bright indirect light in a lean, fast-draining mineral mix, since the reticulation is most pronounced and attractive when the plant is grown hard rather than kept shaded and soft. It forms small clumps over time, and offsets can be divided once they have rooted independently. Water only once the soil has dried fully, withholding water almost entirely through winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; its upright, grass-like growth habit is unusual for the genus and should not be mistaken for a typical flattened rosette.

directions: Restricted to the Witteberg mountain range near Ladismith in South Africa's Western Cape, this unmistakable species abandons the usual flattened Haworthia rosette for dense tufts of narrow, upright, almost grass-like leaves. Grow it in bright indirect light in a gritty, fast-draining mix, as its thin leaves can scorch in hot direct sun more readily than chunkier-leaved relatives. It clumps steadily from the base into multi-headed tufts, so division of rooted offshoots is the standard means of propagation. Allow the mix to dry out fully between waterings and cut back further during the cooler winter rest.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf and stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; this is the largest-growing species in the genus, so give it a wide, shallow container to accommodate its mature rosette size.

directions: Discovered on rocky coastal slopes near San Luis Gonzaga along the Gulf of California in Baja California, Mexico, this species forms by far the largest rosettes in the genus, with broad, thick, pale glaucous blue-green leaves that can reach a foot across on mature plants. Grow it in bright, filtered light to a few hours of gentle direct sun in a mineral-rich, fast-draining mix, since intense exposure in cultivation can scorch the chalky leaf surface. Tall, wiry inflorescences carry small cream to white flowers speckled with maroon in spring. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings and protect it from both prolonged damp and hard frost.
